chief_complaint: sudden appearance of perfectly smooth, circular, completely bald patches on scalp without scaling or inflammation
hpi_details: 26F presenting with well-demarcated non-scarring coin-sized hair loss patches showing 'exclamation mark hairs' at the margin responding to monthly intralesional Triamcinolone acetonide microinjections.
ideas: She thinks the sudden round bald spots are from extreme work stress and tight hair ties pulling her hair out by the roots.
concerns: She is worried that the bald spots will spread until all her hair falls out, forcing her to wear a wig before her sister's upcoming wedding.
expectations: She hopes to receive steroid injections or a fast-acting hair regrowth serum directly into the spots today.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Alopecia Areata is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management of Alopecia Areata is guided by extent of hair loss, typically starting with intralesional or topical corticosteroids for limited patches and escalating for extensive or refractory disease.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden appearance of perfectly smooth, circular, completely bald patches on scalp without scaling or inflammation

Key HPI features: 26F presenting with well-demarcated non-scarring coin-sized hair loss patches showing 'exclamation mark hairs' at the margin responding to monthly intralesional Triamcinolone acetonide microinjections.
Objective/Exam findings: Well-demarcated, smooth, non-scarring bald patch(es) on the scalp with 'exclamation mark' hairs at the margin; no scaling, erythema, or broken hairs of varying lengths.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Alopecia Areata.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Tinea capitis (scaling present) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly progressive total scalp or body hair loss — suggests more extensive disease (alopecia totalis/universalis).
management_principles: Confirm diagnosis clinically (exclamation mark hairs, smooth non-scarring patches); biopsy only if presentation is atypical.
Offer monthly intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injections for limited patchy disease.
Consider topical corticosteroids or minoxidil as adjuncts, and refer to dermatology for extensive or refractory disease.
Counsel on the unpredictable, relapsing-remitting course and screen for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid disease).
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune attack on hair follicles causing sudden, well-demarcated, coin-sized bald patches without scarring or scaling, often with 'exclamation mark' hairs at the border.
red_flags: Rapidly progressive total scalp or body hair loss — suggests more extensive disease (alopecia totalis/universalis)

must_ask.say: How suddenly did this bald patch appear?
Is the skin underneath smooth, or is there any scaling or redness?
How many patches do you have, and where?
Does the area itch or hurt?
Have you had significant stress recently, or any other autoimmune conditions?

history.answer: I noticed a couple of completely bald, round spots on my scalp that appeared out of nowhere.
It started suddenly about three weeks ago when I was brushing my hair and noticed a coin-sized bald spot.
Right now there are two coin-sized round patches near the crown and side of my scalp.
The skin on the patch is completely smooth and bare, like a coin, without any flakes or scabs.
I haven't noticed any thinning of my eyebrows, eyelashes, or body hair at all.

Alert, well-nourished young female sitting comfortably in no acute distress, with hair partially parted to show localized hair loss.
Well-demarcated, smooth, completely bald, coin-sized circular patches on the scalp with exclamation mark hairs at the margins; no erythema, scaling, follicular plugging, or scarring.
Eyebrows and eyelashes are full and intact, with normal conjunctivae and sclerae.
